label: Stop 5: Place Saint-Géry, where Brussels began

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: This one isn't grand. It's a pleasant square, with cafés, and an old brick hall in the middle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it might be the most important stop on the tour, because this is where Brussels started.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Or at least, where the story says it did.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Right. The island.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Remember the river. Before it was buried, the Senne divided into channels here, forming little islands in the marsh.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the tradition is that around the year five eighty, a holy man named Gaugericus, known in French as Saint Géry, who was the bishop of Cambrai, built a small chapel on an island in the river.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Right here?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Close to where you're standing.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The square is named after him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians are cautious, because the sources are later and uncertain, but it's a good candidate for the seed of the city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the name of the city?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The earliest forms look something like Bruocsella.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Most scholars read it as a home in the marsh, or a dwelling by the swamp.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A very honest name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's what a farmer would call a wet bit of ground.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And you're standing on that wet ground.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's just that it's been paved over and covered up.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So that's the story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the story. Around the year nine seventy-nine, Charles, the exiled Carolingian duke, is said to have built a fortification on an island in the river, and moved the relics of Saint Gudula to the chapel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That date is the one usually given for the founding of Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: With a caution.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With a caution. Modern historians say the story rests on sources written long afterward, and that the city probably grew gradually, over several generations.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it's the story that stuck, and Brussels celebrated its thousandth birthday in 1979.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there's an old hall.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The brick building in the middle of the square is the old market hall, the Halles Saint-Géry, and it's close to where the island once was.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the nineteenth century, it was a covered market.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now it's an exhibition and event space, with a cafe, and the square around it is full of bars.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A good place to sit.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A very good place. And it's a nice way to end.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The city started in a swamp, on an island, with a chapel and a market.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It grew into a capital, it rebuilt itself after a bombardment, it buried its river, and now people sit outside in the sun and drink beer on the spot where it began.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It's a sort of full circle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. Take a moment. Order something.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Look at the old hall, and then look at the paving stones and imagine the water.
